title: Votive candles
hookLine: a candle left burning keeps praying after you leave

lines: A NURSE AFTER A NIGHT SHIFT.
A FEW COINS AND A LONG MATCH.
cards: A nurse finishes a night shift and stops at a church that's open early. Near a statue of Mary stands a metal rack of little candles in glass cups, some burning, some burned out.
She drops a few coins in the slot, takes a long match, and lights one. She kneels for maybe a minute, thinking of a patient, a man with no visitors. Then she has to go: sleep, kids, life.
But the little flame stays. It burns all morning while she sleeps, beside others someone lit for a mother, a soldier, a baby, an exam.

teach.h: I AM THE LIGHT OF THE WORLD.
teach.b: A votive candle is lit as a sign of a prayer, for someone or something specific, and left to burn before an image of Christ, Mary or a saint. In your first month, you learned why there's fire in every church.

Here's the root. In John's Gospel, Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims, "I am the light of the world: he that followeth me, walketh not in darkness." So when Catholics light a candle, it isn't decoration.
It points to him. Next, what the candle does, and doesn't.

teach.h: A SIGN, NOT A PRAYER MACHINE.
teach.b: A candle isn't a prayer machine. It doesn't pray instead of you, and a bigger candle doesn't get a better answer. It's a sign: you came, you prayed, and you left something behind that says so.
The prayer was yours; the flame keeps it in view after you've gone back to work. Then, the coins.
The slot is for an offering, which helps pay for the candles and the church. It isn't a price; the prayer never depended on the coins. Who's it for?

Anyone. A Catholic can light a candle for a friend of another faith, or of none, for an enemy, for someone who died long ago, for a person on the news whose name they'll never know. The candle doesn't check credentials.
Last, what it teaches: prayer doesn't end when you stand up.
The Catholic imagination keeps finding small ways to say that, a candle, a medal, a holy water font by the door, each one a reminder you can see.

how: Catholics light votive candles in churches before images of Christ, Mary and the saints, often leaving a small offering, and pray for a particular person or intention; some keep a candle at a home altar.

o: a candle that prays for you while you're away
a candle that lights the altar during Mass
a candle lit as a sign of a prayer for someone

p: what Jesus calls himself in John
a sign of a prayer already made

s: a bigger candle gets a better answer
a candle is a sign of prayer, not a prayer machine.
the coins are the price of the prayer
the offering helps pay for candles and the church. the prayer never depended on the coins.
a Catholic can light a candle for someone of another faith
anyone at all: a friend, an enemy, a stranger on the news.

games.q: you've lit a candle for a sick friend and prayed for a minute. now you have to leave for work. what happens to the prayer?
o: it ends when you stand up.
the candle prays it for you, so you don't need to.
it was yours; the flame keeps it in view.
games.why: the prayer was yours. the flame is a sign that keeps it in view after you've gone.

practice: If you're home and it's safe, light a candle on a table, away from anything that can catch; if not, picture the rack in a church, the long match.
Say one person's name, aloud or inside, and hold them in the light: if you pray, in your own words or with a Hail Mary; if you don't, keep them in mind. Blow it out when you're done.

wordCard.voice: Votive. A candle lit as a sign of a prayer for someone, left burning before an image of Christ, Mary or a saint. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the candle keeps praying. A small flame, still lit after you've gone. I'll be here tomorrow.
